plan.topic: Home blood pressure readings lower months into tirzepatide: what SURMOUNT-1 reported at 72 weeks, and why you never change blood pressure medicines on your own
plan.angle: Sentence 1: 'Home blood pressure cuff reading lower on tirzepatide? Bring those numbers to your doctor.' Sentence 2 card: in SURMOUNT-1, average systolic blood pressure fell more on tirzepatide than on placebo at 72 weeks, using the exact NEJM mmHg figures for both groups, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Label line: 'Among people taking tirzepatide, low blood pressure was reported more often in those also on blood pressure medicines: 2.2% vs 1.2%.' Firm untagged line: never change blood pressure medicines on your own, and review lower readings and any dizziness with your doctor. Untagged: fainting, chest pain or confusion mean your local emergency number. Close with the fixed don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Post note target: L1 once it's verified live, otherwise Side Effects.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide: Blood Pressure Reading Lower at Home? #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1 (After 6 Months covers 72-week blood pressure changes) that drives traffic to the long video. It's a felt home-monitor moment with a contrarian-but-true point: lower readings don't mean adjusting your medicines yourself. | fact-check: Fits the channel and the guardrails: it says outright never to change blood pressure medicines on your own. Checked the label line. The Zepbound label says: "Hypotension was more frequently seen in ZEPBOUND-treated patients on concomitant antihypertensive therapy (2.2%) compared to ZEPBOUND-treated patients not on antihypertensive therapy (1.2%)." This compares tirzepatide users with each other, not tirzepatide with placebo. The card must say so and must not imply a placebo comparison. The SURMOUNT-1 systolic figures must be copied exactly from L1's verified script and NEJM: mean change at 72 weeks, tirzepatide vs placebo, full population, in mmHg. Don't publish S3 ahead of a verified L1 unless the figures were checked on their own. Never imply that lower readings mean you can cut back on medicine. Fix the source date (the HTML label prints 'Revised: 8/2026').

package.title: Tirzepatide and Blood Pressure: What a 72-Week Trial Found #shorts
package.description:
Tirzepatide, 72 weeks in SURMOUNT-1: in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, the average top blood pressure number fell about 7 points on tirzepatide vs about 1 on placebo plus counseling. In the label's pooled weight trials, low blood pressure on tirzepatide was reported in 2.2% of people also on blood pressure medicines vs 1.2% not on them.
Never change blood pressure medicines on your own. Review lower readings, dizziness or fluid loss with your doctor.
Fainting, chest pain or confusion: call your local emergency number.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#tirzepatide
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sentence 2 is the felt cuff moment and the emotional beat ("A lower cuff reading can surprise you. The trial's average fell too."). It doesn't link a viewer's own home reading to the trial, and it doesn't open on a source. Scene 1's card uses the fact-checker's full muted-viewer wording (timeframe, comparator, population), which overrides the 2–6 word card rule. Spoken word count, checked by hand: s1 13, s2 12, s3 36, s4 31, s5 18, s6 10, s7 25, s8 6 = 151 words (standard arm, 135–160).

script.cta: No subscribe line, no link line and no 'full video' line. Closing order: our own emergency line (all three signs on the card), the fixed don't-stop line ('those emergency signs') as two cards, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' as one card, then the loop line. Post-note watch-next target (Exp G): L1 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) After 6 Months: What Happens Next?' once it's verified live, otherwise Side Effects. Packaging: use only the generic name 'tirzepatide' (#tirzepatide) in the title, captions and hashtags. Never present these numbers as Mounjaro or type 2 diabetes data. S2 keeps 'Revised: 8/2026' only while the uspl.lilly.com HTML label is the linked document. If the link switches to DailyMed or the PDF label, cite that document's 'Revised: 11/2026' instead. factcheck.summary:
I checked the figures in this Short against the sources, and they hold up. The script can go ahead once the minor wording fixes below are made.

- **SURMOUNT-1 (S1):** average systolic change at week 72 was −7.2 mmHg on pooled tirzepatide vs −1.0 mmHg on placebo. A search result quoted these NEJM figures (ranges −7.8 to −6.7 and −2.3 to −0.3; difference −6.2 mmHg). The NEJM page itself returned 403, so I confirmed the S1 URL from search results, not by opening it. The population (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes) and "placebo plus counseling" match the craft notes.
- **Label (S2):** the Zepbound HTML label at uspl.lilly.com is printed "Revised: 8/2026". Section 6.1 says: "Hypotension was more frequently seen in ZEPBOUND-treated patients on concomitant antihypertensive therapy (2.2%) compared to ZEPBOUND-treated patients not on antihypertensive therapy (1.2%)." The script's framing (tirzepatide users compared with each other, not with placebo) is correct. The label also gives 1.6% on Zepbound vs 0.1% on placebo, and systolic drops of 6.6–7.7 vs 1.0 mmHg.
- **Word count:** I counted 158 spoken words by hand, matching the log and within the standard arm (135–160).
- **Safety:** the emergency line is our own and has no source tag, the don't-stop line and "Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber." are word for word, and the advice not to change blood pressure medicines alone is clear.

The remaining issues are small: on-screen scope, one card that ends mid-clause, a "full video" line that may promise something that doesn't exist, and a note on the keyword's scope.
